bible_refs.note: Lemma completed from u07-open: Cyril has ταῖς ἀσθενείαις (plural) and ὑπερεντυγχάνει ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, the Byzantine reading; Τὸ τί προσευξόμεθα καθὸ δεῖ οὐκ οἴδαμεν quoted twice more.
Οὕτως οὖν προσεύχεσθε ὑμεῖς· Πάτερ ἡμῶν ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς ... γενηθήτω τὸ θέλημά σου ὡς ἐν οὐρανῷ καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς; Cyril adds καὶ ὅσα τούτοις ἐστὶν ἐφεξῆς.
τὴν ἀπαρχὴν τοῦ Πνεύματος ἔχοντες ... στενάζομεν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς, υἱοθεσίαν ἀπεκδεχόμενοι τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν τοῦ σώματος; Cyril's order is shorter and omits ἡμῶν after σώματος.

Ἃ ὀφθαλμὸς οὐκ εἶδεν καὶ οὖς οὐκ ἤκουσεν καὶ ἐπὶ καρδίαν ἀνθρώπου οὐκ ἀνέβη, ἃ ἡτοίμασεν ὁ θεὸς τοῖς ἀγαπῶσιν αὐτόν. Paul's text itself draws on Isaiah 64:4 (LXX Isaiah 64:3); not cited separately because Cyril quotes Paul.
αἰτεῖτε καὶ οὐ λαμβάνετε, διότι κακῶς αἰτεῖσθε, ἵνα ἐν ταῖς ἡδοναῖς ὑμῶν δαπανήσητε; introduced as 'the Savior's disciple'.
New lemma: Οἴδαμεν δὲ ὅτι τοῖς ἀγαπῶσι τὸν θεὸν πάντα συνεργεῖ εἰς ἀγαθόν, τοῖς κατὰ πρόθεσιν κλητοῖς οὖσιν.
Quotation begins here (Οὐδεὶς δύναται ἐλθεῖν πρός) and is completed at the start of u07-rem-mid (με, ἐὰν μὴ ὁ πατὴρ ὁ πέμψας με ἑλκύσῃ αὐτόν).

choices.term: σοφὸν γάρ ἐστι καθάπερ καὶ ὁ Υἱός
choices.english: the Spirit is wise, just as the Son is
choices.why: σοφὸν γάρ ἐστι καθάπερ καὶ ὁ Υἱός: the neuter σοφόν agrees with Πνεῦμα; rendered “the Spirit is wise, just as the Son is”.

choices.english: a life that is truly approved
choices.why: τὴν εὐδόκιμον ἀληθῶς κατορθῶσαι ζωήν: εὐδόκιμος means well-approved; rendered “a life that is truly approved”; Cyril does not name who approves, so “to God” is not added.
ἀναστοιχειοῦται: literally “is re-elemented”; rendered “is re-formed”. Its subject is the body from the previous clause, given as “it”.
κατὰ πρόθεσιν is kept as “according to purpose” without “his”, because Cyril goes on to ask whose purpose is meant (the caller's or the called's).

pass_a_gloss: [continues lemma Romans 8:26 begun in u07-open] to our weaknesses (ἀσθενείαις, plural) etc. (κ.τ.λ.). But the Spirit itself intercedes-over (ὑπερεντυγχάνει) on behalf of us with groanings (στεναγμοῖς) unspeakable (ἀλαλήτοις). With unspeakable groanings intercedes (ἐντυγχάνει) for us our spirit, clearly (δηλονότι); for we groan sometimes (ἐσθ' ὅτε), being eager (σπουδάζοντες) to make supplications (ἱκετείας) to God. Therefore (οὐκοῦν) in the Holy Spirit we learn this too; for it is wise (σοφόν, neuter: the Spirit) just as also the Son. Since he says: what we shall pray as is necessary (καθὸ δεῖ) we do not know, let us seek (ζητήσωμεν) that. Yet in what manner (τρόπον) one must pray we have been taught beforehand (προπεπαιδεύμεθα) by Christ saying clearly (ἐναργῶς): thus therefore you pray: Father of us in the heavens, hallowed be (ἁγιασθήτω) the name of you, let come the kingdom (βασιλεία), let be done the will (θέλημα) as in heaven also on earth; and what follows in order (ἐφεξῆς). When therefore we have known in which manner it would befit (πρέποι) to make the supplications, what, tell me (εἰπέ μοι), would be the account (λόγος) of the apostolic writings (γραμμάτων)? Or whither would look (βλέποι) what is through Paul's voice? We say then that we pray seeking the request (αἴτησιν) of good things, and before the others things for the glory (δόξαν) of God, and things through which it may be possible to live (βιῶναι) rightly and to achieve (κατορθῶσαι) the well-approved (εὐδόκιμον) life truly; but having the firstfruit (ἀπαρχήν) of the Spirit we ourselves also groan in ourselves awaiting adoption (υἱοθεσίαν), the redemption (ἀπολύτρωσιν) of the body; and as in this part (μέρει) at least, what we shall pray as necessary we do not know. For if eye did not see and ear did not hear and upon heart of man did not go up (ἀνέβη) what God prepared (ἡτοίμασεν) for those loving him, what approaching (προσιόντες) shall we ask? Or how would we know what we have not beheld (τεθεάμεθα), rather even things beyond (ἐπέκεινα) mind (νοῦ) and not known to the hearts of men? Of what kind the redemption of the body, or what the reshaping (μεταπλασμός), and how it is re-elemented (ἀναστοιχειοῦται) into incorruption (ἀφθαρσίαν) and glory, he himself and alone would know, the craftsman (τεχνίτης) of these. The disciple of the Savior said somewhere to some not knowing how they ought to pray: you ask and do not receive, because you ask badly (κακῶς), that you may spend (δαπανήσητε) in your pleasures (ἡδοναῖς). Therefore it would befit, and very reasonably (εἰκότως), those so disposed (διακειμένοις) to say: what we shall pray as necessary we do not know; with unspeakable groanings then we ask in spirit (ἐν πνεύματι) things which we have believed (πεπιστεύκαμεν) will be, but in what manner we are entirely (παντελῶς) ignorant. We know that to those loving God all things work together (συνεργεῖ) for good, to those being called (κλητοῖς) according to purpose (κατὰ πρόθεσιν). All things work together toward the good for those loving God, called according to purpose; but according to the purpose of whom? What would be understood (νοοῖτο) by according to purpose? Then according to purpose would be according to will (βούλησιν); so those about whom the word is have been called according to the will of whom? Whether of the one who has called (κεκληκότος), or also of the called themselves? Therefore every longing (ἔφεσις) carrying (ἀποφέρουσα) us toward righteousness (δικαιοσύνην) would come to us from God and Father; for Christ said somewhere: no one can come toward [continues in u07-rem-mid].
pass_b_english: …our weaknesses, and so on (Romans 8:26). “But the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words” (Romans 8:26). It is our own spirit, plainly, that intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words; for at times we groan when we are eager to make our supplications to God. So this too we learn in the Holy Spirit, for the Spirit is wise, just as the Son is.

But since he says, “We do not know what we should pray for as we ought” (Romans 8:26), let us look into this. And yet we have already been taught by Christ how we ought to pray, for he says plainly, “Pray, then, like this: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as in heaven” (Matthew 6:9–10), and all that follows. Since, then, we know the fitting way to make our supplications, tell me, what would be the sense of the apostle’s words? Or at what would the words spoken through Paul’s voice be aimed?

We say, then, that we do pray, seeking to ask for good things, and before all else for what serves the glory of God, and for the things by which we may live rightly and achieve a life that is truly approved. But “having the firstfruits of the Spirit, we ourselves also groan within ourselves, waiting for adoption, the redemption of the body” (Romans 8:23); and it is in this respect, at least, that “we do not know what we should pray for as we ought” (Romans 8:26). For if “no eye has seen and no ear has heard, nor has it entered the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9), what shall we ask for when we draw near? Or how could we know what we have not seen, or rather, things that lie beyond the mind and are not known to human hearts? What the redemption of the body will be, or what its refashioning is, and how it is re-formed into incorruption and glory, only he who is the craftsman of these things would know.

The Savior’s disciple, too, said somewhere to some who did not know how to pray as they ought, “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your pleasures” (James 4:3). It would therefore be quite fitting, and with good reason, for those in such a state to say, “We do not know what we should pray for as we ought” (Romans 8:26). So with groanings too deep for words we ask in the spirit for things that we believe will come to be, though we are wholly ignorant of the manner in which they will come.

“We know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to purpose” (Romans 8:28). All things do work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to purpose. But according to whose purpose? And what is meant by “according to purpose”? “According to purpose” would mean “according to will.” Then according to whose will have those under discussion been called: that of the one who called them, or also that of those who were called? Now every longing that carries us toward righteousness would come to us from God the Father; for Christ said somewhere (John 6:44), “No one can come to…

reviewer: claude (Wave A review, clause by clause against the Greek)
review_notes: Staged translation checked clause by clause against the source; sense, negation, Scripture IDs (Romans 8:26, 8:23, 8:28; Matthew 6:9–10; 1 Corinthians 2:9; James 4:3; John 6:44) are right. Fixed in tr6.json: (1) εὐδόκιμον ζωήν was 'a life truly pleasing to God' – 'to God' is not in the Greek, now 'a life that is truly approved' (translator note updated); (2) stiff order 'taught how we ought to pray, by Christ, who says' now 'taught by Christ how we ought to pray, for he says'; (3) 'Or where would what is said through Paul's voice be looking?' (calque of ὅποι βλέποι) now 'Or at what would the words spoken through Paul's voice be aimed?'; (4) 'he alone would know who is the craftsman' reordered to 'only he who is the craftsman of these things would know'.
Copy-text: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos via Khazarzar (Fragmenta in sancti Pauli epistulam ad Romanos.pdf).

The row opens mid-lemma: ταῖς ἀσθενείαις ἡμῶν κ.τ.λ. completes Ὡσαύτως δὲ καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα συναντιλαμβάνεται at the end of u07-open, so the English opens with an ellipsis; κ.τ.λ. rendered “and so on”. It ends mid-quotation (John 6:44), completed at the start of u07-rem-mid; the closing ellipsis marks the break. Nothing supplied.

Spirit in the Romans 8:26 lemma is capitalised as Scripture and to match the end of u07-open. Cyril then glosses it as τὸ ἡμῶν δηλονότι πνεῦμα, “our own spirit, plainly”, and says this too is learned “in the Holy Spirit”; ἐν πνεύματι in “we ask in the spirit” is left lowercase because it follows that gloss of the human spirit.
σοφὸν γάρ ἐστι καθάπερ καὶ ὁ Υἱός: the neuter σοφόν agrees with Πνεῦμα; rendered “the Spirit is wise, just as the Son is”.
τὴν εὐδόκιμον ἀληθῶς κατορθῶσαι ζωήν: εὐδόκιμος means well-approved; rendered “a life that is truly approved”; Cyril does not name who approves, so “to God” is not added.
ἀναστοιχειοῦται: literally “is re-elemented”; rendered “is re-formed”. Its subject is the body from the previous clause, given as “it”.
κατὰ πρόθεσιν is kept as “according to purpose” without “his”, because Cyril goes on to ask whose purpose is meant (the caller's or the called's).
PG column numbers 219 and 220 and the page number 19 are dropped from the reading text.
